parole.significato: Forms adjectives, mostly from nouns, the adjectives having the sense "similar to"; -like.
parole.testo: From Low German achtich (“equipped with”), hachtich.
Via Low German -erie, from Old French -erie, from Latin -aria.

parole.significato: denotes a person or thing with a characteristic property or function
parole.testo: From Low German -ert, from Old Saxon -hart, -hard.

parole.significato: Denotes a woman occupied with an activity, especially a profession.
parole.testo: From Low German -sche, a noun suffix in the feminine of the adjective suffix -sch, corresponding to Old Norse -skr, see Danish -sk. The suffix mixed with the feminine suffix -se of Old French -esse.

From Low German and Middle Low German bricke, ultimately from the root of brække (“to break”).

From Low German verpurren. Equivalent to for- + purre.

parole.significato: to confuse; to disturb, mix up, bewilder

From Low German frech (“naughty, barefaced”).
From Low German vulborden.
From Low German vulenden and German vollenden.

From Low German letke, a diminutive of Middle Low German latte, German Latte (“lath”), from Old Saxon latta, from Proto-West Germanic *lattu (“board, bar”). Cognate with English lath.

From Low German schinke, from Middle Low German schinke, from Old Saxon skinka, from Proto-West Germanic *skinkō.

From Low German schuf, from the Middle Low German verb schûven, from Old Saxon *skiovan, from Proto-West Germanic *skeuban (“to drive, push”).
From Low German schör (“weak, fragile”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *skuriz, derived from the verb *skeraną (“to cut”). Norwegian Bokmål skjør and Swedish skör are also borrowed from Low German.
From Low German slagge, derived from a cognate to slå (“strike, hit”). See English slag for more information.
From Low German sludern, from a group of words derived from Proto-Germanic *slūm- (“loose, slack, flabby”), such as English slumber. Compare also Dutch slodderen (“to be sloppy”).

parole.significato: an ill-mannered, dishonest (young) man; a punk.
